asks: A labelled diagram of three equal strips, one cut into halves with one half shaded, one cut into thirds with one third shaded, and one cut into sixths.
A drawing of two equal paper strips lying one under the other, the first folded into halves and the second into thirds, both marked again into six equal parts.
picture.why: Strips of the same length make it plain that halves and thirds are pieces of different sizes, and that sixths are a size both can be cut into.

big_idea.text: To add fractions with different denominators, first cut both into pieces of the same size, then count the pieces.

objectives.can: Add two fractions with different denominators by changing them to the same denominator
Explain why the numerators and denominators cannot simply be added
Judge whether an answer to a fraction sum is sensible

why_it_matters.text: Half a cup of milk and a third of a cup of water, or half a roti and a third of another, are amounts you put together every day.

the_why.text: Halves and thirds are pieces of different sizes, so they cannot be counted together; cutting each half into three and each third into two turns both into sixths, pieces of one size, which can be counted.

picture.text: Two equal strips: one with a half shaded, one with a third shaded. Both strips are then cut into six equal parts: the half becomes 3 sixths and the third 2 sixths. The shaded parts slide onto a third strip, filling 5 of its 6 parts.

card.diagram_ask: A labelled diagram of three equal strips, one cut into halves with one half shaded, one cut into thirds with one third shaded, and one cut into sixths.

needs_first.text: What the top and bottom numbers of a fraction mean.
Equivalent fractions: 1/2 is the same amount as 3/6.

mistakes.why_it_fails: 2/5 is less than 1/2 alone, so it cannot be a half with something more added; the bottom number names the size of the pieces and is not added.

mistakes.mistake: Changing the bottom number without changing the top: 1/2 becomes 1/6.
mistakes.why_it_fails: 1/6 is a much smaller amount than 1/2; when each piece is cut into three, the number of shaded pieces must also become three times as many.

mistakes.mistake: Adding the bottom numbers and keeping the top: 1/2 + 1/3 = 1/5.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Fifths are smaller pieces than either halves or thirds, so 1/5 is less than either of the fractions being added.

opening_question.question: You eat half a roti and then a third of another roti of the same size. Have you eaten more or less than one whole roti, and how much?
guesses: A bit less than one roti
opening_question.answer: 5/6 of a roti: a little less than one whole.

route.what: Show the half strip and the third strip and ask how much they make together. Ask for a guess.
Try 2/5: put 2/5 of a strip next to the half strip. It is shorter than the half alone, so it cannot be right.
Ask: why can we not just count the pieces? Because one half and one third are pieces of different sizes.
Cut each half into three and each third into two: both strips are now in sixths. The half is 3 sixths and the third is 2 sixths.
Slide the shaded sixths onto one strip: 3 + 2 = 5 of 6 parts are shaded.
Name it: make the denominators the same (a common denominator), then add the numerators: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
1/4 + 1/2: cut the half into two quarters, so 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.
2/3 + 1/4: the learner cuts both into twelfths and finds 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12 before it is shown.
The learner says why the pieces must be the same size before they are added.

questions.question: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
questions.explain: A half is 3 sixths and a third is 2 sixths, so together they make 5 sixths.

questions.question: Riya says 1/4 + 1/2 = 2/6. Is that sensible?
options: No: 2/6 is less than 1/2 alone, and the answer is 3/4
No: the answer is 1/6, because 1/2 becomes 1/4
questions.explain: Adding more to a half must give more than a half; with quarters, 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

try_it.title: Strips in sixths
materials: two strips of paper 12 cm long
try_it.stands_for: Each 12 cm strip is one whole; a mark every 2 cm cuts it into sixths.
try_it.predict: Will one half and one third together cover more than the whole strip, exactly the whole, or less?
steps: On the first strip shade one half (6 cm); on the second shade one third (4 cm).
Mark both strips every 2 cm so each is cut into six equal parts.
Count the shaded sixths on each strip.
Lay the strips end to end so the shaded parts touch and measure the shaded length.
try_it.observe: The half is 3 sixths and the third is 2 sixths; together the shaded parts are 10 cm, 5 sixths of one strip, a little less than the whole.
try_it.question: Why did you mark both strips in sixths before adding?
try_it.expected: Because a half and a third are pieces of different sizes, and only pieces of the same size can be counted together; sixths fit exactly into both, so 3 sixths and 2 sixths make 5 sixths.
try_it.write: Before adding fractions, make the pieces the same size. 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
try_it.in_class: Pairs, each with two 12 cm strips. The teacher draws two strips on the board, one in halves and one in thirds, and asks the class to mark the sixths. Ask: is 1/2 + 1/3 more or less than one whole? A class that says 2/5 is still adding tops and bottoms.
